newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire government tries to quell panic in capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire government tries to quell panic in capital.

text.p: The Zairean government tried on Monday to quell fears of an imminent coup and halt speculation that President Mobutu Sese Seko may be dying in hospital in Europe.

But against the expectations of most Kinshasa residents no major decisions or changes were announced by the cabinet which met in emergency session two days after the fall to rebels of Zaire's third city Kisangani.
Travel agents reported a rush of flight bookings by Zaireans keen to leave the capital. Planes to Europe or South Africa, where Zaireans need no visa, were the most popular.
"The government invites the people not to panic as this is both unjustified and fed by pure rumour," the cabinet said in a statement signed by its spokesman Jean-Claude Biebie Ekalabo.
The fall of Kisangani, nerve centre for army operations in the war zone, coincided with rumours over the weekend suggesting that Mobutu may be about to die.

One senior official told Reuters that government ministers and Mobutu allies were the most affected and panicked by the rumours of the president's deteriorating health and increasing concern over the loyalty of troops and their commanders.
"The government is keen to reassure public opinion on the state of the president's health," the cabinet said.
Mobutu had been admitted to hospital in Monaco for "a final check", continued to carry out his functions and would return home this week, it added.
The veteran Zairean leader, who seized power in 1965, has spent most of his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery there in August.

Residents in Kisangani say that the city, headquarters for army operations in the war zone, fell to rebels after Zairean soldiers looted what they could and fled. Hundreds of defeated government troops surrendered their arms to rebels on Monday.

The cabinet said Ugandan troops attacked the army in Kisangani, forcing it to retreat. It said Ugandan army regulars had been sent as reinforcements and were "heavily equipped with both men and sophisticated weapons".
The defence minister, it added, was examining the situation with the intention of regaining the initiative in the conflict.

Kinshasa residents reported sporadic gunshots overnight on Sunday around the teeming capital, where rumours of an imminent coup attempt are rife. In one incident, armed men opened fire from a car in the opposition stronghold of Limete.
In Kinshasa's central market, traders prepared to transfer their goods to safe houses, anticipating the mayhem that has regularly occurred after rebels have defeated the army.
"It's the habit of our soldiers to start looting so we have to take precautions," one said.
Some opposition newspapers called for the resignation of the government and Mobutu.
"Mobutu and (Prime Minister) Kengo (wa Dondo) must be chased away," the hardline opposition Elima newspaper proclaimed.
"The whole of Zaire is falling like a ripe fruit," The Soft newspaper headlined. "Should the war be pursued?" it asked.
Monday's government statement made no mention of talks with the rebels.
The government, which has accepted a U.N. ceasefire plan, has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading in support of the rebels. All three deny the charge.
